subsection: 4. Elements and principles of design in clothing

notes.b: The elements are the visual building blocks of a garment, and each can be changed to alter the look of the outfit. There are five: line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.
points: Line: a visible edge or direction in a garment, created by seams, necklines, hemlines, trims, pleats, fastenings and pattern. Where the eye is led along a line, the garment seems to go in that direction.
Shape: the outline of a garment or of an area within it, such as a neckline, sleeve or pocket. The outline of the whole garment is its silhouette.

Colour: hue (the actual colour), tone (how light or dark it is) and intensity (how bright or dull it is). Warm colours such as red and orange appear to advance, while cool colours such as blue and green appear to recede.
Colour schemes can be monochrome or tonal (one colour in different shades), contrasting or complementary. Colour should also suit the wearer's skin, hair and eye tones.
Texture: the surface quality of a fabric, which can be smooth, rough, shiny or matt, and which can be seen or felt.
Pattern: the repetition of line, shape or colour over a surface, such as stripes, checks, herringbone, zig-zag, polka dots, florals or geometric prints.
notes.tip: Keep the two lists apart: elements are the building blocks (line, shape, colour, texture, pattern) and principles are how they are arranged. Use only these five elements, because the marking schemes list five and other terms can lose marks.

notes.h: Line and its effect on the figure
notes.b: Because the eye follows lines, the direction of the lines in a garment changes how tall, wide or soft the wearer appears. Designers use this to flatter the figure.
points: Vertical lines give the impression of length, so they make the figure look slimmer and taller.
Horizontal lines draw the eye across the body, which makes the figure look wider and shorter.
Diagonal lines add contrast and movement, and they lead the eye across the garment.
Curved lines soften an outfit and add a feminine feel, such as the curve of a rounded neckline.
A princess seam runs from the shoulder or armhole to the hem. It shapes the garment to the body without a waist seam, and the long unbroken line also helps the wearer look taller.
notes.tip: In a question on line, name the direction and say what it does to the eye and the figure: vertical adds height and slimness, horizontal adds width.

notes.b: Colour and texture change how much light a garment reflects or absorbs, and that changes how big the wearer appears. Remember that these are effects on appearance only.
points: Dark colours appear to reduce the size of the figure because they absorb light, while light and bright colours appear to enlarge it. Dark navy and black also define and slim the silhouette.
One colour worn from head to toe, or tonal shades of one colour, creates a longer, unbroken line, so the figure looks taller. Tonal shades also add depth.
Contrasting or complementary colours at the top and bottom divide the outfit and can balance the shape of the figure, for example when the shoulders and hips are different widths.
Shiny fabrics reflect light and increase the apparent size of the figure, while matt fabrics absorb light and reduce it.
Rough, thick or heavily textured fabrics look bulkier, while smooth fabrics give a neater, more streamlined finish.
notes.tip: Say that dark colours make the body appear smaller, not that they shrink it. Examiners reward the reason, so add that dark colours absorb light and light colours reflect it.

notes.b: Pattern and shape work in the same way as line and colour: they decide where the eye goes and how wide or narrow the figure looks.
points: Small patterns suit small figures, and a larger figure can carry a large pattern well.
Vertical stripes add height, and horizontal stripes add width and draw attention to the middle of the figure.
A patterned area draws the eye to the place where it is worn, for example near the face or neckline for the upper body or at the hem.
Narrow rectangular shapes slim the figure, while triangular or A-line shapes widen the hem or shoulders and so can balance the hips or shoulders.
A fitted bodice with a full skirt gives an hourglass shape, and a fitted top with straight trousers gives a streamlined shape.
notes.tip: When asked how pattern affects appearance, link the pattern to its size or direction and say what it does to the eye.

notes.b: The principles describe how the elements are arranged to create a unified garment. There are five: proportion, balance, emphasis, harmony and rhythm.
points: Proportion: the relationship between the sizes of the parts of a garment, to each other and to the wearer, such as pockets sized to the garment, a collar sized to the neckline, or jacket length to skirt length.
Balance: an even distribution of visual weight. It can be vertical, symmetrical (both sides match) or asymmetrical (the sides differ but still feel even).

Emphasis: a centre of interest that draws the eye to one area, created by a brooch, contrasting trim, a belt, a bright accessory, a bold hemline or a neckline. There should be only one centre of emphasis in an outfit.
Harmony (unity): the sense that all parts of a design work together and complement one another, for example colours, fabrics and style that suit each other, or one colour repeated.
Rhythm or repetition: the repeated use of a colour, line or shape, such as a repeated button or stripe, which moves the eye through the garment.
Diagram: when asked to sketch an outfit, label the elements and principles used, such as line, shape, proportion, harmony and emphasis.
notes.tip: Never stop at a definition. Name the principle, then say how it is shown in this particular outfit, for example emphasis through a contrasting blazer or bright trim. Use one centre of emphasis only, because competing focal points spoil it.

notes.h: Using design to flatter body size and shape
notes.b: Choosing the elements well lets a wearer look taller, slimmer or better balanced, and draw attention to a feature or away from one. This is the use of the elements that exam questions ask about directly.
points: To look taller or slimmer, use vertical lines, one colour head to toe or tonal shades, dark colours such as navy and black that absorb light, V-necks, princess seams, a single long line from shoulder to hem and narrow shapes.
To balance or add width, use horizontal stripes, light or bright colours and bulky textures. Contrasting top and bottom colours balance the shoulders and hips.
To draw attention to a feature, put pattern or a bright colour near it, such as near the face for the upper body, or use a belt to define the waist.
To draw attention away from an area, wear dark colour over it, because dark colours appear to reduce size.
Colour also flatters the wearer's hair, eyes and skin; for example, blues can brighten the complexion.
Shape, fit and proportion matter too: choose lines that suit the figure. A short jacket with slim trousers lengthens the leg line.
notes.tip: For flattering body size and shape, cover colour, line and pattern: darker reduces, lighter increases, one colour gives height, contrast balances, and line and pattern direct the eye.

notes.h: Applying the elements and principles to garment construction
notes.b: The way a garment is made creates its line, shape and emphasis. Here the focus is on the effect of each feature on the design.
points: Seams join the parts of a garment, and their placement creates line and can add shaping to the body.
Darts remove excess fabric to shape a garment around the bust, waist or hips. Pressing defines the darts.
Princess seams shape the garment without a waist seam.
Pleats, tucks and gathers add fullness and movement, and are used at the waist, sleeve or skirt, where they can add visual interest.
Pockets, collars, buttons, trims and fastenings add line and emphasis, and they must be positioned in proportion to the garment.
Fabric choice affects the finished design: crisp fabrics hold a shape, as in tailoring, while soft fabrics drape. The fabric's texture and pattern must also suit the design lines.
Design and colour can be applied to fabric by dyeing, screen, roller, stencil or transfer printing, embroidery and appliqué (fabric shapes stitched on).

notes.b: A garment is evaluated against three criteria: how well its design serves its function, its comfort and its aesthetic appeal. Examiners often set these as headings for an outfit shown in a picture.
points: Function: the garment must suit the purpose, activity, climate, weather and occasion it is intended for, such as freedom of movement for sport. Durability, easy care, useful pockets and fastenings that work also count.
Comfort: the fabric (soft, absorbent, breathable or stretch), fit and ease of movement, weight, versatility in different weather and footwear determine whether the wearer is comfortable.
Aesthetic appeal: the colour scheme, line, shape, texture, proportion, balance and emphasis, and any accessories, must work together to produce an attractive and pleasing overall look.
A well-designed garment shows a clear relationship between its design features and the function they serve, for example a drawcord hood, reflective trim or a zip opening.
Using colour and design to flatter the body: choose colours and lines that emphasise the wearer's best features and balance any areas they wish to de-emphasise.
Other headings that appear are shape, proportion, design features, current fashion trend, lifestyle, cost, care and suitability for the occasion.
Method: for each heading make a point from the picture, then give the reason, such as the fabric, cut or colour.
notes.tip: Spread your points across every heading; two points per heading is typical. Draw each from the picture, for example loose fabric and stretch for comfort, or pockets and durable crease-resistant fabric for function, with the reason.

keyTerms.definition: The basic visual components of a garment: line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.
The ways in which the elements are arranged, including proportion, balance, emphasis, harmony and rhythm.
The relationship between the size of one part of a garment and the size of another part or of the whole.
The creation of a focal point that draws the eye to one area of a garment.
The sense that all the parts of a design work together and complement each other.
The movement of the eye through a garment created by the repetition of a colour, line or shape.
A stitched fold of fabric that removes excess material to shape a garment around a body curve.
A long seam running from the shoulder or armhole to the hem that shapes a garment without a waist seam.

factCards.definition: Line, shape, colour, texture and pattern.

factCards.term: Three effects of vertical lines on the figure
factCards.definition: They give the impression of length, make the figure look slimmer and taller, and draw the eye upward.

factCards.term: Two effects of light colours on the figure
factCards.definition: They advance and enlarge the figure, making it look bigger.

factCards.term: Three criteria for evaluating a garment

factCards.definition: They add width to the figure and draw attention to the middle of the body.

factCards.term: Two functions of darts and pleats in construction
factCards.definition: Darts remove excess fabric to create shape around the body, and pleats add fullness and movement to a skirt or sleeve.

factCards.term: Three ways to achieve balance in a design
factCards.definition: Symmetrical, asymmetrical and vertical balance, each of which distributes the parts of a design differently.

questions.prompt: Name three elements of design and state how one of them can be used to make a short figure look taller.
questions.model: Three elements: line, colour and texture. Line can make a short figure look taller by using vertical lines, such as a long open jacket, a princess seam or a column of buttons, which give an impression of length. Dark, matt colours in the outfit can also help the figure look longer, because they recede and reduce the visual size of the body.

questions.prompt: Explain how the principles of emphasis and proportion can be applied to the design of an outfit for a formal occasion.
questions.model: Emphasis: a focal point such as an embellished neckline, a contrasting brooch or a bold hemline draws the eye to one feature, and the rest of the outfit is kept simpler so that the focal point stands out. Proportion: the sizes of the parts are in balance with each other and with the wearer, for example a single colour running from neckline to hem creates an unbroken line, and pockets, collars and trims are sized to suit the garment. A well-proportioned outfit looks harmonious and suits the occasion.
